opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that "education" may be the wrong frame for children that young, at least if by education we mean the kind of thing that happens in school — sitting still, being told facts, practicing skills that someone else has decided are important. What we've learned from developmental science over the last thirty or forty years is that very young children are already extraordinarily powerful learners. They're like little scientists, constantly exploring, experimenting, testing hypotheses about how the world works and how other people work. In some ways they're better learners than we are, precisely because they're less constrained by what they already know.

So the right kind of environment for a child under seven is one that supports that natural exploration rather than replacing it. That means lots of free play, lots of opportunity to mess around with things, to pretend, to ask questions, and crucially, to be around caring adults who are paying attention to them. A lot of the most important learning at that age is happening through apprenticeship and imitation — watching what the grown-ups around them do and trying it out — rather than through explicit instruction.

There's actually some nice experimental work on this. In one study, when an adult acts like a teacher and says, "Here's how this toy works," children will learn that one thing and stop exploring. When the adult is more ambiguous, the children go on to discover all sorts of other things the toy can do. So direct instruction has real costs as well as benefits. It narrows the space of possibilities.

I'd also emphasize that this is a period when what children most need is a secure, stable relationship with the people who care for them. That's the foundation for everything else. The evolutionary picture is that we have this long, protected childhood precisely so that children can explore without having to worry about getting things done. Childhood is a kind of research and development phase for the species, and adulthood is production and marketing. When we try to push the production-and-marketing mindset down into preschool — worksheets, flashcards, academic drilling — I think we're really misunderstanding what that period of life is for.

r001.rationale: The response says education for children under seven should support their natural exploration, with free play, experimentation, and asking questions, rather than relying on direct instruction.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that we have a really deep misconception about what children under seven are doing, which is that we think of them as sort of defective adults who need to be shaped into students. And I think the picture that comes out of the developmental research is almost the opposite. Young children are the best learners we know of in the universe, and the way they learn is not by sitting in a classroom being instructed. It's by exploring, by playing, by watching the people around them, by doing what I sometimes call "messing about."

So if you ask what the right education is for a four-year-old or a five-year-old, my answer is that it should look very little like school as we usually imagine it. It should be a rich, safe environment with lots of interesting things to act on, lots of other children, and caring adults who are doing things that the children can observe and imitate and participate in. That's actually how humans have raised children for most of our history. Kids learned by being around adults who were cooking or making tools or taking care of babies, and they got to take part in it.

What I'm much more skeptical about is the push to get formal academic instruction into those early years. There are studies, for example, where if you directly teach a child how a toy works, they learn exactly that thing and then they stop exploring. Whereas if you let them figure it out, they discover all the other things the toy can do. So the worry is that early didactic schooling buys you a little bit of short-term performance on narrow measures at the cost of exactly the broad, flexible, exploratory learning that's the whole point of childhood. There's some evidence that the gains from early academic programs fade by second or third grade while kids who had play-based preschools do just as well or better in the long run.

Now, I want to be careful. "Play-based" doesn't mean neglect. The thing that really matters for young children is having stable, attentive caregivers and a world that's interesting and not too dangerous. If you've got that, children will pretty much educate themselves, in the sense that matters. The job of adults is less to be teachers and more to be, I sometimes say, gardeners rather than carpenters. You're not building a product to specification. You're creating the conditions where something can grow.

r001.rationale: The response says children under seven learn through exploring, playing, and figuring things out, and recommends a rich environment that supports this instead of formal instruction.

astra-6.text:
I think children under seven need lots of opportunities to play, to explore, and to interact with other people—both children and adults. We tend to think of education as something an adult does to a child: You have some information, and your job is to get it into the child’s head. But young children are already extraordinarily good at learning. The question is how to give them an environment that lets those abilities flourish.

That doesn’t mean leaving them alone. It means having caring, attentive adults who talk with them, read with them, answer their questions, and give them interesting things to do. It means opportunities to pretend, to make things, to go outside, to discover that something they thought would work doesn’t work.

I’d be much more concerned about whether a young child has that rich, secure environment than whether they’re getting an early start on worksheets. Play isn’t simply a break from learning. For young children, it’s one of the central ways learning happens.

r001.rationale: The response recommends opportunities to explore, ask questions, and discover how things work as appropriate education for children under seven.

sol-6.1.text:
I think children under seven need lots of opportunities to play, to explore, and to interact with people who care about them. That can sound like saying they don’t need to learn anything, but it’s almost the opposite. Play is one of the ways young children learn the most. They’re experimenting: What happens if I do this? What could this object be? What would it be like to be somebody else?

So I’d want an environment that’s rich in things to investigate and people to talk to, with adults who are attentive and engaged. Read with children, tell them stories, take them outside, let them build things and make things up. There’s a role for adults in helping them discover something they wouldn’t have discovered on their own. But that’s quite different from organizing their lives around lessons and getting the right answer.

The temptation is to think that if formal instruction is useful at eight, we should start it at four. But young children have particular strengths as learners, and we should give those strengths room to develop.

r001.rationale: The response endorses play, exploration, experimentation, and investigating as ways young children learn, which clearly supports inquiry-based education for children under seven.
